# Areal models


## Conditional autoregressive models {.smaller background-color="#FFFFFF"  auto-animate="TRUE"}

:::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Markov in Space:**

First order conditional autoregressive model or a CAR(1) model.

- Every node is conditionally dependent on its four nearest neighbours

![](figures/markov.png){fig-align="center" width="293"}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: incremental
- Models based on neighbourhood have a name in statistics: they are **Markovian models**

- Markovian models are specified entirely through "*neighbourhood structures*"

![](figures/mp1.png){fig-align="center" width="423"}

:::
:::
::::

## Modelling spatial similarity {.smaller auto-animate="TRUE"}

Example of a GMRF we covered

::: callout
## ICAR/Besag model

$$u_i|\mathbf{u}_{-i},\tau_u, \sim N\left(\frac{1}{d_i}\sum_{j\sim i}u_j,\frac{1}{d_i\tau_u}\right)$$

- $\tau_u$: precision parameter proportional to the number of neighbours.

- $d_i$ is the number of neighbours

$$\mathbf{u}|\tau_u \sim N\left(0,\frac{1}{\tau_u}Q^{-1}\right),$$

Where $Q$ denotes the precision matrix defined as

$$Q_{i,j} = \begin{cases}
d_i, & i = j \\
-1, & i \sim j \\
0, &\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}$$
:::

## Modelling spatial similarity {.smaller auto-animate="TRUE"}



Example of a GMRF we covered

::: callout
## ICAR/Besag model

$$u_i|\mathbf{u}_{-i},\tau_u, \sim N\left(\frac{1}{d_i}\sum_{j\sim i}u_j,\frac{1}{d_i\tau_u}\right)$$
:::

::: callout
## BYM

$$\begin{aligned}
v_i &= \underbrace{u_i}_{\text{ICAR}} + \underbrace{z_i}_{iid}\\
z_i|\tau_z &\sim N(0,\tau_{z}^{-1})
\end{aligned}$$
 - Higher $\tau_u$ values lead to stronger smoothing (less spatial variability).

- Lower $\tau_u$ values allow for greater local variation.
:::

::: fragment
- To compare smoothness we need to *scale* the model (this is **NOT** done by default in the definition of the `besag` model in `inlabru`)
- For disconnected graphs (or graphs with islands) some care is needed when defining the sum-to-zero constraints
:::

## Modelling spatial similarity {.smaller auto-animate="TRUE"}


Example of a GMRF we covered

::: callout
## ICAR/Besag model

$$u_i|\mathbf{u}_{-i},\tau_u, \sim N\left(\frac{1}{d_i}\sum_{j\sim i}u_j,\frac{1}{d_i\tau_u}\right)$$
:::

::: callout
## BYM

$$\begin{aligned}
v_i &= \underbrace{u_i}_{\text{ICAR}} + \underbrace{z_i}_{iid}\\
z_i|\tau_z &\sim N(0,\tau_{z}^{-1})
\end{aligned}$$
:::

::: callout
## BYM 2

$$    \mathbf{b} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\tau_b}} \left(\sqrt{1-\phi}v^*+\sqrt{\phi}u^*\right).$$

- The precision $\tau_b>0$ controls the marginal variance contribution of the weighted sum $u^*$ and $v^*$.

- The mixing parameter $0 \leq \phi \leq 1$ measures the proportion of the marginal variance explained by the structured effect $u^*$

$$\begin{aligned}
P(1/\sqrt{\tau_b} > U) &= P(\sigma_{\tau_b} > U) = \alpha\\
P(\phi < U) &= \alpha
\end{aligned}$$
:::

# Non-linear predictors

## Extending INLA to non-linear predictors {.smaller}

::: smaller
In addition to being a wrapper around R-INLA, `inlabru` extends the scope of INLA to models with non-linear predictors $\tilde{\eta}(\mathbf{u})$.
:::

. . .

::::::: columns
:::: {.column width="70%"}
::: smaller
:bulb: **The idea** :bulb:

- Linearize $\tilde{\eta}(\mathbf{u})$ using a first-order Taylor expansion around $\mathbf{u}_0$:

$$
\tilde{\eta}(\mathbf{u}) \approx \tilde{\eta}(\mathbf{u}_0) + f_{\text{linear}}(\mathbf{u}) = \bar{\eta}(\mathbf{u})
$$

- Run INLA for the linearized problem\
- Iterate until convergence
  - $\tilde{\eta}(\mathbf{u}_0)$ close enough to $\bar{\eta}(\mathbf{u_0})$
:::
::::

:::: {.column width="30%"}
::: {.callout-note .smaller}
**Note**

For details:\
<https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.00791v1>
:::
::::
:::::::


## Extending INLA to non-linear predictors

- The linearization is an approximation on top of the "usual" INLA approximation
- Accuracy will depend on the nature of the non-linearity around $\mathbf{u}_0$ and the choice of convergence criteria.
- Greater care than usual is needed for the choice of priors.


. . .

Some checks are possible (see the arxive paper)...

**BUT** this method is still in an "experimental" mode, so great care is needed!


## Example {.smaller}

$$
\begin{align}
y_t &\sim\mathcal{N}(\eta_t,\sigma^2)\\
\eta_t &= L(1-\exp(-k(t-t_0)))\\
L &\sim\exp(1/300); \qquad k \sim\exp(2);\qquad t_0\sim\exp(1)
\end{align}
$$

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| code-line-numbers: "1-2|3-17|9-13|15-22"
#| 
scale_par <- sd(df$y)
df <- df %>% mutate(y_scale = y / scale_par)

cmp <- ~ -1 +
  L(1, prec.linear = 1, marginal = bm_marginal(qexp, rate = scale_par / 300)) +
  kappa(1, prec.linear = 1, marginal = bm_marginal(qexp, rate = 2)) +
  t0(1, -1, prec.linear = 1, marginal = bm_marginal(qexp, rate = 1))

growth_function <- function(L, kappa, t0, age) {
  L * (1 - exp(-kappa * (age - t0)))
}

formula <- y ~  growth_function(L, kappa, t0, age)

lik <- bru_obs(
  formula = formula,
  family = "gaussian",
  data = df
)
bru_options_set(bru_verbose = 1, bru_max_iter = 20)
fit <- bru(cmp, lik)
```
